# R5 Digest — Absalom the Rebel (2 Sam 13–14)

**Source slice:** `R5_absalom_rebel_13-14_7702-8448.txt`  
**Raw lines covered:** 7702–8448 (slice-internal lines 1–747)  
**Scope:** Tsumura NICOT on 2 Sam 13:1–14:33 — Amnon–Tamar; Absalom’s vengeance and exile; wise woman of Tekoa; Absalom’s return without full reconciliation  
**Attribution:** All claims are Tsumura’s (commentary + translation choices) unless marked as his citation of another scholar  
**Targets pool:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[amnon]], [[tamar]], [[joab]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-01
**Claim:** Chapters 13–14 (“Absalom the Rebel”) function as prologue to “Absalom’s Rebellion” in chs. 15–20; even though Tamar and Amnon dominate 13:1-22, the section is principally about Absalom (named at the start, v. 4, and vv. 20-22). Tamar is introduced as Absalom’s sister, not as David’s daughter.  
**Quote:** “this section is principally concerned with Absalom… Tamar is introduced as Absalom’s sister, not as David’s daughter. Thus, chapters 13-14 (“Absalom the Rebel”) serve as a prologue to “Absalom’s Rebellion” in chapters 15-20.”  
**Locus:** §A intro; 13:1-22 framing (slice ll. 1–7)  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[absalom]], [[tamar]], [[amnon]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-02
**Claim:** 13:1-22 is an account of rape and incest; the brother-sister relation is referred to a dozen times. The rape is an “outrageous thing” (nebālāh-type language; Gen 34:7; Deut 22:21; Judg 20:6; Jer 29:23), “not done in Israel,” with national implications because it occurs in the royal family.  
**Quote:** “This is an account of rape and incest — the brother-sister relationship between Tamar and Amnon is referred to a dozen times. This rape was an “outrageous thing”… which was “not done in Israel,” and since it occurred in the royal family, it had implications for the whole nation.”  
**Locus:** §1 Amnon and Tamar intro (slice ll. 9–11)  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[amnon]], [[tamar]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-03
**Claim:** Tamar was Absalom’s full sister (children of David and Maacah) and Amnon’s half-sister; Amnon was David’s eldest son. She may have been named after David’s ancestress (Gen 38).  
**Quote:** “Tamar was Absalom’s full sister, both of them being children of David and Maacah, which meant she was the half-sister of Amnon, David’s eldest son. Tamar may have been named after David’s ancestress; see Gen 38.”  
**Locus:** 13:1-2 notes (slice ll. 24–26)  
**Targets:** [[tamar]], [[absalom]], [[amnon]], [[david]], [[2-samuel]]

### C-R5-04
**Claim:** Amnon’s “love” is better described as lust; Hitpael “make himself sick” appears only in this chapter (vv. 2, 5, 6); they lived in different houses and would probably not have met except in public.  
**Quote:** “Amnon’s “love” could better be described as “lust.”… They lived in different houses, and probably would not have met except in public.”  
**Locus:** 13:2 notes (slice ll. 28–32)  
**Targets:** [[amnon]], [[tamar]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-05
**Claim:** Jonadab (Amnon’s cousin, son of Shimeah/David’s elder brother) is ḥākām used negatively as “shrewd/crafty”; he later stays home when Amnon is assassinated (v. 32).  
**Quote:** “here, it is used in a negative sense as “shrewd” or “crafty.” Jonadab later was wise enough to stay home when Amnon, his “friend,” was assassinated by the command of Absalom (v. 32).”  
**Locus:** 13:3 notes (slice ll. 84–86)  
**Targets:** [[amnon]], [[absalom]], [[david]], [[2-samuel]]

### C-R5-06
**Claim:** lebābôt (food Tamar prepares) relates to “heart” / “hearten” and Song 4:9 libbabtînî; Tsumura prefers “dumplings” (boiled dough-balls) over “cakes” because of *bšl “boil” (v. 8) and “pour” (v. 9).  
**Quote:** “so the food was probably some type of dumplings, that is, boiled dough-balls. This is supported by the use of the verb “to pour” in v. 9.”  
**Locus:** 13:6-7 notes (slice ll. 90–94)

**Quote:** “It apparently never occurred to David to be suspicious, and Tamar, of course, would obey her father.”

### C-R5-08
**Claim:** Tamar’s protest (13:12) is poetic AXB parallelism emphasizing nebālāh as the key concluding word; “such a thing is not done in Israel” parallels Shechem’s rape of Dinah (Gen 34:7).  
**Quote:** “For the expression such a thing is not done in Israel, see the similar language used in the case of Shechem’s rape of Dinah in Gen. 34:7. The disgraceful thing (nebālāh…) is not simply a “foolish” (*nbl) thing. It is used especially of sexual misconduct such as rape…”  
**Locus:** 13:12 notes (slice ll. 142–152)  
**Targets:** [[tamar]], [[amnon]], [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-09
**Claim:** Brother–sister intercourse (even half-siblings) is forbidden in Lev 18:9; given the stress on outrage, the prohibition was likely accepted then. Tamar’s “speak to the king, he will not withhold me” may mean David would bend the rules—or she is only trying to escape.  
**Quote:** “Intercourse between brother and sister, even half-brother and half-sister, was forbidden in Lev. 18:9… Perhaps Tamar is saying here that David would be willing to bend the rules, or perhaps she is just trying to escape.”  
**Locus:** 13:13 notes (slice ll. 154–156)  
**Targets:** [[tamar]], [[amnon]], [[david]], [[2-samuel]]

### C-R5-10
**Claim:** Amnon overpowers Tamar and rapes her: “he would not listen to her and was stronger than she and violated her and lay with her” (Tsumura’s translation of 13:14).  
**Quote:** “But he would not listen to her and was stronger than she and violated her and lay with her.”  
**Locus:** 13:14 translation (slice ll. 134)

### C-R5-11
**Claim:** Amnon’s post-rape hatred exceeds his former “love”; Tsumura calls this an archetypal “blame the victim” mentality (contemptuous “this woman,” v. 17).  
**Quote:** “This hatred and contempt (“this woman,” v. 17…) can be said to be an archetypal example of “blame the victim” mentality.”

### C-R5-12
**Claim:** Per Exod 22:16 / Deut 22:28-29, a man who raped an unbetrothed woman could not divorce her; Tamar protests that sending her away is a greater wrong than the rape. Her sentence is interrupted (aposiopesis) by Amnon’s command to the servant.  
**Quote:** “Tamar seems to be protesting that Amnon’s action of sending me away is much worse than raping her. But, her word of protest was interrupted by his command to his servant… this is an example of aposiopesis…”  
**Locus:** 13:16 notes (slice ll. 186–188)  
**Targets:** [[tamar]], [[amnon]], [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-13
**Claim:** Amnon’s mixed plural/singular imperatives (“Send… and lock”) may show reluctance to own thrusting her out—spreading responsibility via the plural. Contemptuous ʾet-zōʾt “this [woman].”  
**Quote:** “it might be that Amnon knew how wrong he was and was reluctant to order his servant to do the wrong of thrusting her out, and so used the plural imperative form for the first verb send to spread the responsibility around.”  
**Locus:** 13:17 notes (slice ll. 190–192)  
**Targets:** [[amnon]], [[tamar]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

**Quote:** “v. 18a was probably placed here intentionally as a literary insertion (AXB)… One can picture Tamar’s resistance as she was forced outside.”

### C-R5-15
**Claim:** Tamar mourns with ashes, torn gown, hand on head, continual crying; Absalom uses sexual euphemism (“Was… with you?”; cf. ### C-R5-16
**Claim:** David becomes very angry but does nothing—Tsumura’s key judgment on David’s indecisiveness as father/judge and source of later problems. Heads of households must deal justly among household members.  
**Quote:** “David became very angry, but he did not do anything. This sentence conveys how indecisive David was with regard to his sons, the source of much of the later problems. Heads of households have to deal justly among members of their household.”  
**Locus:** 13:21 notes (slice ll. 234)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[amnon]], [[absalom]], [[2-samuel]]

### C-R5-17
**Claim:** LXX (and some reconstructions of 4QSama) adds that David would not punish Amnon because he loved him as firstborn; McCarter et al. claim MT haplography. Tsumura, citing Herbert, finds the reconstruction uncertain and thinks the LXX addition later explains David’s inaction.  
**Quote:** “It seems more natural that this was added later to the LXX to explain David’s action, or rather lack of action.”  
**Locus:** 13:21 notes (slice ll. 234–236)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[amnon]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[2-samuel]]

**Quote:** “In these three verses, the name Absalom appears four times, hinting that he will become the major character in the subsequent story.”

### C-R5-19
**Claim:** After two years, Absalom uses sheepshearing feast at Baal-hazor (near Ephraim; modern Jebel ʿAsur) to invite all the king’s sons; he likely invited David first expecting refusal, to color the request for Amnon without suspicion. David eventually lets Amnon and all the sons go.  
**Quote:** “Probably Absalom invited David, guessing that he would decline, in order to lend color to the request for his brothers to come. If he had started out by asking for Amnon to come, it could have been suspicious.”  
**Locus:** 13:23-27 notes (slice ll. 239–276)

### C-R5-20

**Quote:** “For only Amnon is dead! For according to Absalom’s command this has been decided since the day when he violated his sister Tamar.”

### C-R5-23
**Claim:** Against almost all modern translations that read 13:39 as David “longing/pining” for Absalom, Tsumura (with McCarter’s logical point that Joab’s ruse would be unnecessary if so) reads: King David’s [desire] to go out **against** Absalom was over (he was comforted about Amnon’s death). Brachylogy of omitted nepeš (fem.) explains feminine verb.  
**Quote:** “The sentence seems to mean, King David’s [desire] to go out against Absalom finished… “if David longed for Abishalom, Joab’s ruse in 14:1ff. would not be necessary.””

McCarter’s inclusio of Tekoa woman with wise woman of Abel (ch. 20) around rebellion is noted; Tsumura finds the present situation more similar to ch. 12: wise messenger (prophet there, woman here) tells a mashal so David may realize his real problem.

### C-R5-25
**Claim:** Against McCarter/Budde rearranging vv. 8-14 and 15-17, Tsumura retains MT order: vv. 4-7 (A) and 15-17 (B) frame real message 8-14 (X)—AXB with suspense, tension, and relief.

### C-R5-27
**Claim:** Hebrew “the heart of the king [was] on Absalom” need not be positive longing (contra NASB/NIV); given 13:39 as end of desire to go out against Absalom, lēb is David’s state of mind—he was thinking about the matter. Joab pushes acceptance without later being Absalom’s partisan.  
**Quote:** “the Hebrew… does not necessarily imply that his thoughts were positive… He was just thinking about the matter. Joab decides to push the king toward accepting him, though later he does not show himself to be particularly a partisan of Absalom.”

### C-R5-28
**Claim:** Joab fetches a wise woman from Tekoa (Khirbet Tequʿ, ~10 mi S of Jerusalem; Amos’s hometown; near Bethlehem, Joab’s home area). Her speech compares with Abigail (1 Sam 25) and the wise woman of Abel (2 Sam 20). Joab puts words in her mouth.  
**Quote:** “Though it is not certain whether Tekoa was one of the centers of wisdom tradition in ancient Israel, Joab brought a wise woman from there. The speech of this wise woman of Tekoa can be compared with that of two other women in Samuel, Abigail… and the wise woman of Abel…”  
**Locus:** 14:2-3 notes (slice ll. 404–406)  
**Targets:** [[joab]], [[david]], [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-29
**Claim:** The mashal asks David to set aside ordinary death-penalty for murder (Num 35:31 etc.) for the family’s good—widowhood and sole heir. Even under centralized kingship, the kin group (hammišpāḥāh / hāʿām) still handles domestic homicide.  
**Quote:** “the woman appeals to the king to set aside the ordinary laws demanding the death of a murderer… not because of any extenuating circumstances in the killing, but for the good of the family… even though Israel at the time was a centralized state… the kin group dealt with a case of domestic homicide.”  
**Locus:** 14:5-7 notes (slice ll. 450–464)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[absalom]], [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-30
**Claim:** **Intertextuality critique (Lyke / Bergen, not Bakhtin):** Lyke’s “two sons” sibling-rivalry topos across biblical/nonbiblical pairs is “full of speculation, based on later Jewish traditions.” Bergen sees “too much” Cain–Abel similarity without differences. Shared motifs (“two sons,” “in the field,” one kills the other) reflect universal sibling rivalry (also extrabiblical) and East Mediterranean blood-revenge custom—not tight literary dependence. Differences: Cain’s murder planned; woman’s story a sudden quarrel; Absalom’s case closer to Cain’s planned murder though not David’s only sons.  
**Quote:** “His explanation is full of speculation, based on later Jewish traditions… Bergen also seems to see too much in the similarities… the reason for such correspondences is due to the universal nature of sibling rivalry… Cain’s murder of Abel was planned, but in the woman’s story it seems to have been a sudden quarrel. Absalom’s case is more similar to Cain’s murder in this aspect…”  
**Locus:** 14:6 notes (slice ll. 452–462)  
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[absalom]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-31
**Claim:** “Heir” language suggests Absalom was popularly considered heir (oldest surviving son); woman’s plea that kinsmen would extinguish her “coal” (hope for family) and eliminate the heir is meant to lead David to his postponed reconciliation and royal concern for the heir who would sit on his throne (cf. 7:11b-16).  
**Quote:** “Apparently, Absalom was now considered the heir, at least in popular sentiment… Therefore, it is the purpose of the woman to remind David that he as the Lord’s anointed king should be concerned with his heir who would sit on his throne after him…”  
**Locus:** 14:7 notes (slice ll. 466–468)  
**Targets:** [[absalom]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[2-samuel]]

### C-R5-32
**Claim:** In the framed message (X: 14:8-14), the woman presses to a real charge: by not bringing back his banished one, the king is guilty and has “plotted this thing against the people of God.” She then stands with the king before God (“we will surely die…”) and claims God will not take away life but will devise plans so the banished one will not remain banished—king should act as God’s human agent.  
**Quote:** “king David is “guilty” here since he has not “planned [devices]” to bring back “his banished one,” while God “will devise plans so that the banished one will not remain banished.””  
**Locus:** 14:13-14 notes (slice ll. 514–558)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[absalom]], [[joab]], [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-33
**Claim:** David may already identify the woman’s problem with Absalom emotionally; “the one who has spoken to you” (v. 10) is ambiguous (clan spokesman or Joab who sent her)—David may already suspect Joab’s device. Royal oath “not one hair of your son shall fall” protects the fictitious son and also Absalom (McCarter noted; Tsumura accepts).  
**Quote:** “David may have already suspected Joab’s device and so purposefully used this ambiguouse phrase on purpose… this solemn royal oath “now protects the fictitious son of the Tekoite woman and also . . . his own son Abishalom.””  
**Locus:** 14:8-14 / 11 notes (slice ll. 536–548)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[joab]], [[absalom]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R5-34
**Claim:** Woman finishes by returning to her clan story (B: 15-17); “inheritance of God” = people/land of Israel or family’s share—if son dies, no representative among future generations. Flattery “angel of God” reflects king as Yahweh’s earthly judicial representative. David then forces admission that Joab commanded her to change the course of the matter.  
**Quote:** “In order to change the course of the matter your servant Joab has done this thing… my lord is wise, like the wisdom of the angel of God, to know all that is in the earth.”

**Claim:** Absalom has three (unnamed) sons—probably died young, given 18:18—and one daughter Tamar (beautiful; MT/4QSamc vs LXX “Maacah”). ### C-R5-41
**Claim:** Structural synthesis of David’s failures across 13–14 (Tsumura): (1) no suspicion when sending Tamar to Amnon; (2) anger without judicial action after rape; (3) passivity enabling Absalom’s two-year revenge plot; (4) incomplete recall—face withheld for two more years—until Absalom’s arson forces full audience. Indecision with sons is “the source of much of the later problems.”  
**Quote:** “This sentence conveys how indecisive David was with regard to his sons, the source of much of the later problems… David recalls him, but his forgiveness is incomplete…”  
**Locus:** 13:21; 14:24, 28-33 (slice ll. 234, 676, 738–742)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[absalom]], [[amnon]], [[tamar]], [[joab]], [[2-samuel]]
